demo.title: Same network, no attack
demo.blurb: Another day on the same network (simulated, 10 minutes): a new device joins, and the internet router is swapped for a backup router with a different MAC address. There is no attack: ARPGuard should stay calm.

alerts.message: 192.168.1.12 moved from f4:f5:d8:6e:21:12 to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 2s after a DHCP ACK
gateway 192.168.1.1 is now claimed by 20:4e:7f:c4:08:01; trusted MAC is 50:c7:bf:3a:1c:01

confidence.basis: the address changed only once and traffic stayed normal

alerts.message: 192.168.1.12 moved from f4:f5:d8:6e:21:12 to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 2s after a DHCP ACK

explanation.headline: 192.168.1.12 now belongs to a new Espressif device; this looks harmless
explanation.what_happened: At 4:22, 192.168.1.12 moved from f4:f5:d8:6e:21:12 to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 (Espressif). This looks like a normal change because the router's DHCP server gave this address to the new device 2 seconds earlier. The AI model found only 12 of 655 packets around it unusual, which is ordinary background noise. ARPGuard writes it down and treats the new device as the owner from now on.

attacker.reasoning: No attacker: this looks like a normal change, because the router's DHCP server gave this address to the new device 2 seconds earlier.

impact: Nothing expected. Other devices update their address books within a few minutes

confidence.reason: the address changed only once and traffic stayed normal

fixes.action: Check that the change was expected
fixes.detail: Ask whoever manages the device. A new device, a new network card or a replaced router explains a one-time change. Write it down.
This gives the switch a trusted list of which device owns which IP, which DAI needs. Only the port that leads to the router should be trusted.
fixes.command:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
interface Gi0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust

confidence.basis: the address changed only once and traffic stayed normal

alerts.message: gateway 192.168.1.1 is now claimed by 20:4e:7f:c4:08:01; trusted MAC is 50:c7:bf:3a:1c:01

explanation.headline: 192.168.1.1 now belongs to a new Netgear device; this looks harmless
explanation.what_happened: At 6:40, 192.168.1.1 moved from 50:c7:bf:3a:1c:01 to 20:4e:7f:c4:08:01 (Netgear). This looks like a normal change because the old device went quiet before the new one appeared, and the traffic stayed normal. The AI model found only 24 of 810 packets around it unusual, which is ordinary background noise. ARPGuard writes it down and treats the new device as the owner from now on. The old device was last heard from 1 seconds before the change.

attacker.reasoning: No attacker: this looks like a normal change, because the old device went quiet before the new one appeared, and the traffic stayed normal.

impact: Nothing expected. Other devices update their address books within a few minutes

confidence.reason: the address changed only once and traffic stayed normal

fixes.action: Check that the change was expected
fixes.detail: Ask whoever manages the device. A new device, a new network card or a replaced router explains a one-time change. Write it down.
This gives the switch a trusted list of which device owns which IP, which DAI needs. Only the port that leads to the router should be trusted.
fixes.command:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
interface Gi0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust

caveats: This is the router's address. A single change usually means the router was replaced or restarted, but please confirm: a one-off fake answer would look the same.
